title: Basic Selectors & Grouping 🎯
description: Master type, class, ID, universal selectors, and how to combine them efficiently.

slides.title: Recap: The Core Selectors 🧱
slides.content:
# Your Styling Toolkit You've already used type, class, and ID selectors. Let's solidify them: - **Type selector:** `p { }` – selects all `

` elements. - **Class selector:** `.highlight { }` – selects any element with that class. - **ID selector:** `#logo { }` – selects the unique element with that ID. - **Universal selector:** `* { }` – selects every element (use with care). These are the foundation. Combine them with other selectors to precisely target elements.

slides.title: Grouping Selectors 📦
slides.content: Apply the same styles to multiple selectors by separating them with commas:

quizData.question: What character separates selectors in a grouped rule?
quizData.explanation: Commas allow you to apply the same declaration block to multiple selectors.

slides.title: Compound Selectors 🔗
slides.content:
# Be More Specific Without a Space

Chain selectors together to target elements that match all conditions:
```css
a.highlight { /* <a> elements with class highlight */ }
#main.visible { /* element with id main AND class visible */ }
```
No space between them means the element must satisfy every part. This increases specificity and precision.

slides.title: Compound Selectors in Action
slides.content: Style a button that also has a specific class:

quizData.question: `div.highlight` and `div .highlight` select the same elements.
quizData.explanation: `div.highlight` (no space) selects `<div>` elements with class highlight. `div .highlight` (space) selects elements with class highlight that are descendants of a `<div>`.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content:
## Use Classes as Your Primary Hooks

For styling, rely on classes. IDs are too specific and can't be reused. Classes give you flexibility and keep specificity low.
